title: Match a Grid by Quarter Turns
statement:
You get two square grids of the same size, grid and target, filled with 0 and 1.

You may turn grid clockwise by 90 degrees as many times as you like, including zero times. Return true if some number of turns makes it equal to target cell for cell, and false otherwise.

Only rotations are allowed. Flipping the grid over (a mirror image) does not count.

examples.why: Two quarter turns move the top-left corner to the bottom-right corner.
Three clockwise turns, which is the same as one counter-clockwise turn, put the top row on the left side.
The target is the left-right mirror of grid. Both have three 1s, but none of the four rotations matches.

constraints: 1 ≤ n ≤ 10, both grids are n × n
hints: There are only four distinct orientations: 0, 90, 180 and 270 degrees. A fifth turn brings you back to the start.
Work out where cell (i, j) ends up after one clockwise turn. Look at a 3 × 3 grid with a single 1 in it.
After one clockwise turn, the new cell (i, j) holds the old cell (n − 1 − j, i). Rotate, compare, and repeat at most four times, or check all four orientations with formulas in a single pass.

explain.intuition:
Rotating four times brings the grid back to where it started, so there are only four candidates to test. The work is getting one rotation right.

Turning clockwise, the first column read from bottom to top becomes the first row. In index terms, the new cell (i, j) holds the old cell (n − 1 − j, i). The other orientations follow the same way: 180 degrees reads (n − 1 − i, n − 1 − j) and 270 degrees reads (j, n − 1 − i). Instead of building rotated copies you can check all four formulas against target at once and keep a flag per orientation. It is the same index math a CSS rotate(90deg) does to pixel coordinates.
steps: Keep four flags, one per orientation, all starting as true.
For every cell (i, j) of target, compare it with grid[i][j], grid[n−1−j][i], grid[n−1−i][n−1−j] and grid[j][n−1−i].
Clear a flag as soon as its orientation disagrees with target.
Return true if any flag is still set.
pitfalls: Using the transpose as the rotation. A transpose is a mirror across the diagonal; you also need to reverse each row to get a clockwise turn.
Comparing only the number of 1s. A mirror image has the same count but is not a rotation, as in the third example.
Rotating in place and then forgetting that the grid has changed when you test the next orientation.

complexity.space: O(1) for the formula version, O(n²) when building rotated copies

solutions.title: Rotate and compare four times
solutions.idea: Build the clockwise rotation of the current grid, compare it with the target, and repeat. Four tries cover every orientation.

solutions.title: Check all four orientations in one pass
solutions.idea: Each orientation is just a different way of reading grid's indexes. Keep one flag per orientation and clear it on the first mismatch.

followups: Rotate an n × n grid clockwise in place, with O(1) extra memory.
Also allow mirror flips. How many distinct orientations are there now?
